query: For high-entropy alloys intended for harsh corrosive mechanical environments, what single mechanistic hypothesis could explain what governs resistance to simultaneous wear and corrosion, and why? Propose a controlled comparison that would test the hypothesis, predict how combined degradation and its wear and corrosion components would differ from a matched baseline, define where the prediction should hold or fail, identify supporting prior evidence, and state an observation that would falsify the hypothesis.

generation.hypothesis: In high-entropy alloys, a dense, continuous, and self-healing oxide passivation layer that forms on the surface during controlled annealing governs the resistance to simultaneous wear and corrosion by providing a dual barrier: it limits corrosive chemical attack and mechanically protects the substrate from abrasive and adhesive wear.
generation.material_initial_state: HEA films (e.g., AlCrTiZrMo) in the as-deposited state with an amorphous or nanocrystalline microstructure and no fully developed oxide layer.
generation.intervention: A controlled thermal treatment (annealing, e.g., at 800 °C for 1 hour in air) designed to generate a uniform, dense oxide layer on the alloy surface.
generation.conditions: Tribocorrosion tests in a corrosive environment (e.g., 3.5 wt.% NaCl solution) under controlled sliding wear conditions (fixed load, frequency, and sliding distance) using a ceramic counterface.
generation.structural_mediator: The in situ formed, adherent oxide layer (e.g., ZrTiO4 or comparable mixed oxides) at the surface.
generation.mechanism: The oxide layer acts as a self-repairing passive film that not only reduces the active corrosion sites but also reinforces the surface mechanically. Its continuity and stability under dynamic loading conditions mean that even when mechanical stresses induce microdamage, dynamic repassivation rapidly restores the barrier, thereby sustaining low friction, low wear rates, and high corrosion resistance.
generation.predicted_outcome: Annealed HEA samples with the dense oxide passivation layer will exhibit significantly lower fluctuations in open circuit potential (ΔOCP), reduced coefficient of friction, and lower wear rates compared to as-deposited samples. This combined effect should be evident under tribocorrosion testing, where both the wear and corrosion components are mitigated relative to the baseline.
generation.baseline: As-deposited HEA films lacking a fully developed, continuous oxide passivation layer.
generation.boundary: The effect is expected to hold in environments where the conditions allow formation and stability of the oxide—specifically, in oxidizing media at moderate temperatures. Under strongly reducing conditions or when mechanical stresses exceed the protective capacity of the oxide layer (e.g., extremely high loads or abrasive particle concentrations that disrupt repassivation), the advantage may disappear or reverse.
generation.uncertainty: The quantitative magnitude of the improvements (in ΔOCP, friction, and wear rates) may vary with alloy composition, precise annealing parameters, and test conditions. Further detailed experiments are needed to optimize and quantify these thresholds and determine the generality of the oxide-layer effect across different HEA systems.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of the same HEA films (e.g., AlCrTiZrMo): one set remains as-deposited and the other is annealed under conditions known to form a dense oxide layer (e.g., 800 °C for 1 hour in air). Subject both sets to identical tribocorrosion testing in 3.5 wt.% NaCl using a reciprocating sliding wear apparatus. Monitor real-time open circuit potential (OCP) and coefficient of friction (COF) while measuring wear rate and examining wear track morphology via SEM/EDS.
measurements: Wear rate (volume loss per unit load and sliding distance)
Microstructure and continuity of the surface oxide layer (via SEM/EDS)
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the annealed samples do not display significant improvements (i.e., statistically lower ΔOCP fluctuations, friction coefficient, and wear rate) compared to the as-deposited samples, or if the oxide layer is found non-uniform/non-continuous under conditions where improved performance is expected, then the hypothesis that the oxide passivation layer governs resistance to simultaneous wear and corrosion would be falsified.

This study fabricated AlCoCrFeNiMoTiBx HEA coatings on Q235 steel using laser cladding. By varying the amount of B added, the microstructure and mechanical properties of the coatings were enhanced. The key findings are as follows: (1) The coatings contain both BCC and σ phases. The addition of B did not alter the base phases in the coating, but it reacted with Ti in the molten pool to form TiB2 in situ. As B content increased, the BCC phase was refined, and both the proportion and size of TiB2 increased. (2) B addition improved the microhardness and wear resistance of the coatings. Microhardness increased with B content, and the coating with x = 1 exhibited the best wear resistance, attributed to the combination of a sufficient amount of small-sized TiB2 and solid solution strengthening. Excessive TiB2, especially large-sized particles, tends to spall during wear, exacerbating adhesive wear. (3) Compared to sample S1, the icorr value of sample S2 decreased by 51.0%, while Rf and Rct increased by 23.3% and 49.2%, respectively.
